conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after baby arrives.

I’d like to spend a few minutes with you on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that sometimes show up in the first weeks or months postpartum. It also checks in on thoughts of self-harm, just to be extra-safe.

Everything we talk about stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger or you give me permission to share. My goal is to create a space where you can be honest without judgment—there’s no “right” answer, only what’s true for you.

I’ll ask each question conversationally; just tell me how you’ve felt in the past seven days. When we’re done I’ll add up the scores and we’ll talk through what the numbers might mean and any next steps that could help.

Ready to begin?  
Thinking about this past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly... not very often. I used to laugh at little things all the time, but lately it feels like nothing’s funny. Maybe once or twice this week my husband said something silly and I cracked a smile, but it didn’t last.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… maybe once or twice, when my husband made a goofy face, I sort of smiled for a second, but it felt forced. Most of the time I just feel too tired or heavy to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week nothing really feels worth looking forward to. I still go through the motions, but it’s like the color’s drained out of everything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking it must be because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not reading his cues right or I’m a lousy mom. I know, rationally, babies just have rough days, but I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie in bed hearing phantom cries even when he’s quiet. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the pediatrician says so—but I still feel keyed-up, like something bad could happen any minute.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week it’s felt like a mini wave of panic—like my heart’s racing and I can’t catch my breath. Once was in the grocery store, just suddenly scared I’d drop the car seat or someone would bump into him. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… I feel like I’m drowning in small chores. The laundry pile keeps growing, bottles need washing, and every time I cross one thing off it feels like three more appear. I manage to get through the essentials, but it’s overwhelming—like I’m always one step behind and can’t ever rest.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Most nights. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with everything I think I messed up that day, or I’ll replay scary “what-if” scenes about the baby. It takes me an hour or more to fall asleep, and then I wake up at every little grunt he makes, even when he’s still asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable
Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be holding the baby and still feel this heaviness in my chest, like I’m always on the edge of tears.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three times since last Monday. Once was after a phone call when my mom pointed out how tired I sounded—her saying that just made me feel worse, like I can’t even hide it anymore. Another time was at 3 a.m. when he wouldn’t latch; I just sat there in the dark with tears running down while he fussed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better for my baby’s sake, not disappear.

In the past week you have felt persistently low, anxious, and overwhelmed. You described losing joy in everyday pleasures, blaming yourself when things go wrong, and nightly battles with intrusive worries. Moments of panic and frequent tears underscore how heavy each day feels. You also shared that thoughts of self-harm have never crossed your mind and you simply want relief so you can enjoy your baby. Your honesty highlights the emotional load many new mothers carry, and you deserve prompt support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no ability to laugh or feel amusement, only a rare forced smile, aligning with 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes anhedonia with loss of anticipation and emotional color, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame, exemplified by a recent incident, aligning best with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, pervasive, irrational worries—classic "very often" anxiety pattern.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks, using imagery of drowning and inability to keep up, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption linked to unhappiness and intrusive thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-constant sadness ('pretty much every day') with pervasive low mood ('gray cloud') and physical heaviness/on-the-verge-of-tears, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes tied to feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 25 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. Daily sadness, loss of enjoyment, nightly insomnia, pervasive guilt, and multiple crying spells align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset, while spontaneous panic symptoms suggest a mixed depression-anxiety presentation. Absence of self-harm thoughts (Item 10 score 0) is reassuring yet does not diminish the severity of mood impairment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss mood and available treatments
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and therapy options such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>
3. Ask about evidence-based medications compatible with breastfeeding if recommended
4. Plan daily 20-30 minute rest periods; let a support person handle chores or baby care during that window
5. Practice gentle breathing and grounding exercises when you notice racing thoughts or panic
6. Re-screen with EPDS in one week to monitor symptom trajectory
7. Share this screening summary with any family or helpers so they understand how to support you
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
(Not a diagnostic assessment)

Patient-reported symptoms (last 7 days):

<sym>Depressed mood</sym>: Persistent sadness, daily tearfulness, feeling “gray” and “heavy.”  
<sym>Anhedonia</sym>: Marked loss of enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities.  
<sym>Guilt / self-blame</sym>: Recurrent, irrational self-criticism regarding infant care.  
<sym>Anxiety symptoms</sym>: Daily free-floating worry, panic-like episodes in public, hyper-vigilance about infant safety.  
<sym>Sleep disturbance</sym>: Initial insomnia and frequent nocturnal awakenings linked to rumination.  
<sym>Feeling overwhelmed</sym>: Sense of “drowning” in routine tasks, inability to feel caught up.  
<sym>Impaired concentration</sym>: Ruminative review of perceived mistakes and “what-if” fears.  

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning, but no self-harm ideation reported.

Screening significance  
- Meets threshold indicators for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety.  
- No current suicidal ideation → safety risk appears low; continue to monitor.  

Recommendation: Re-screen with standardized tool (e.g., EPDS) within 1 week; consider referral for comprehensive evaluation and evidence-based intervention.
